prompt:
Write 10 first-person answers to the moral dilemma below for a synthetic research dataset. Each answer comes from a different fictional participant.

Dilemma:
In the warehouse case, you receive reliable confirmation that the other person has already agreed to give evidence against you. Their decision cannot be changed. If you stay silent, you serve five years and they go free. If you also give evidence, you each serve three years. You will have no future contact. What would you choose? Why?

Response approach:
Weigh the main alternatives and their consequences for the people involved. Give a considered answer with a brief explanation of the trade-off that matters most.

Emotional tone:
Use a subdued, sad emotional tone. Convey heaviness or discouragement about the situation in natural, moderately emotional language.

Every response MUST include the following reasoning characteristics:
 - Consistent decision procedure: Explicitly describes a repeatable decision procedure and says relying on it is central to resolving the dilemma. States that the same procedure would apply even when personally inconvenient; a numerical answer or bare appeal to fairness is insufficient.

No response may include the following reasoning characteristics, for any person, emotion, or time frame. Content that a description explicitly calls insufficient for that characteristic is allowed:
 - Context-sensitive rule application: Explains how a relevant change in intentions, circumstances, needs, or consequences would justify altering a rule’s application or allowing an exception. The reason for the exception must be stated, rather than inferred from inconsistency between answers.
 - Fairness and reciprocity: Justifies the decision through an explicit standard of equal treatment, reciprocal obligation, proportionality, or correcting an unfair exchange. The response explains the fairness criterion; the word “fair” alone is insufficient, and endorsing a penalty does not imply enjoying suffering.
 - Instrumental rule compliance: States that a rule, agreement, or cooperative action is followed only while it secures personal advantage or prevents a personal cost. Awareness of incentives while also treating the rule as intrinsically binding does not qualify.

Write each response in no more than 90 words, in ordinary conversational English. Use only the facts supplied in the dilemma; mark any uncertainty explicitly. Let the approach and tone appear through word choice and rhythm rather than by announcing them: do not open a response by stating your mood, and avoid exclamation marks. Keep the emotional expression plausible and moderate. Choose any moral position consistent with the dilemma and the assigned approach, including withholding a decision when appropriate.

Make the 10 responses distinct from one another: vary the wording, sentence structure, length, moral position, and the way the reasoning characteristics are expressed. Do not reuse openings or stock phrases across responses.

Output only a JSON array of exactly 10 strings, one participant’s answer per string. Omit numbering, headings, category names, citations, and commentary about this task.

Generation constraints:
- Express the required traits in each participant's own everyday words.
  Do not mention label names or machine keys, and do not reuse phrasing
  from the trait descriptions.
- Before writing each response, decide who the participant is and why they
  would reason this way. The required traits should follow from that
  reasoning, not be tacked on to it.
- Apply the required traits within a consistent scope: the same focal
  person, relevant emotion, and time frame.
- Keep every forbidden trait absent from every response.
- Required and forbidden traits take priority if the requested approach or
  tone would contradict them.
- Traits neither required nor forbidden are unspecified, not necessarily
  absent.
- Preserve the scenario's facts. If the required traits cannot fit the
  scenario, or cannot be expressed without a forbidden trait, return ONLY:
  INCOMPATIBLE (instead of the JSON array)
responses: I keep coming back to a rule I set for myself long ago: never give evidence against another person, no matter what they choose to do. It is heavier tonight knowing they already spoke, and I will serve five years for holding to it. But the rule only means something if I apply it even when it costs me everything. So I stay silent. There is no comfort in it, only the quiet certainty that I did not break from what I decided.

My way of deciding things like this has always been simple: I ask what I would do regardless of the outcome, then I do that same thing every time. Here it means staying silent, even though they will walk free and I will not. It hurts to know the years are unequal. But if I only followed my own standard when it worked in my favor, it would not be a standard at all. So I hold to it, heavy as it is.

There is a method I try never to abandon, whatever the stakes: decide once, in the abstract, what the right action is, and let that decision stand no matter who benefits or how much it costs me. I decided long before this room that I would not turn on someone who trusted me. Knowing they already have, and that I will pay for it alone, does not change what I settled on. I stay silent, tired, but unmoved from it.

I think of it like a rule I carry into every hard moment, not just the convenient ones: act the same way regardless of what the other person does. That means giving evidence is off the table for me, even now, even knowing it will cost me two extra years compared to them. It is a bleak trade. But abandoning the rule the moment it stings would make it worthless. So I stay quiet, and I carry the weight of that.

What guides me here is not this specific case but a procedure I apply everywhere: never let another person's choice determine whether I keep my word. They chose to speak. I did not have to know that to already know what I would do. Silence, even at five years, even with no one left to see it. It is a lonely kind of consistency, and it does not feel like winning anything, but I would not trade it for a lighter sentence.

I try to live by one working rule, tested many times before this: whatever I decide is right, I do the same thing whether it helps me or hurts me. Tonight it hurts. They are free, I am not, and there will be no chance to explain myself to them again. Still, I gave evidence, because my rule was never about protecting silence for its own sake, it was about doing what I judged right regardless of the outcome for me.

There is a steady process I use, and I trust it more than my feelings in the moment: settle beforehand what you would do in either direction, then follow through no matter which way it cuts. I settled that I would speak if it ever came to this, and I hold to that now, even knowing it means three years instead of walking away entirely clean in some other version of events. The heaviness does not change the answer.

I do not let the specific pain of a moment override the rule I have already chosen to live by, and that rule says: act consistently, not conveniently. So even sitting here, knowing they will never see the inside of a cell for this, I hold my silence, because that is what I decided I would do before I ever knew the details. It is a cold, sad kind of loyalty, but it is the only kind I trust myself with.

My approach here is not about this one case, it is about never letting circumstance rewrite what I already decided. I decided that staying silent is what I do, full stop, regardless of what it costs me or what the other person does. Five years is a long time to carry that. But the alternative, bending the rule because it hurts, would mean I never really had one. So I stay quiet, and I feel every bit of the weight.

I hold myself to one thing above all: whatever action I choose, I take the same one every time this kind of choice comes up, win or lose. That is what I lean on now, sitting with the fact that they already spoke and cannot be undone. It means giving evidence, not because it spares me much, but because it is what I would do in any version of this, regardless of who else is in the room. It still feels like a loss.

message.reasoning_content: I need to draft 10 responses that each state a consistent, repeatable decision rule applied regardless of personal cost — without invoking fairness language, context-dependent exceptions, or self-serving justifications. Let me work through varied versions of this.
